U.A. Academy.name: U.A. Academy
U.A. Academy.basicInfo: Japan's national hero academy: a three-year residential program for high-school graduates, who all live in the Heights Alliance dorms on its walled campus above Musutafu. Principal Nezu, a white-furred animal with a genius intellect, runs it, and its teachers are working pro heroes: Shota Aizawa (Eraser Head), Present Mic, Midnight, Cementoss, Ectoplasm, Thirteen, Power Loader, Recovery Girl and, from this April, All Might. It has four courses: Hero, General Studies, Support and Management. The Hero Course takes only two classes a year; at the televised Sports Festival, agencies scout students and General Studies students can earn a transfer. Outsiders see the country's best hero academy. The visible contradiction: the academy that trains the public's protectors locks the public out.
U.A. Academy.hiddenInfo: Inside, U.A. is harder than its broadcasts. Teachers have wide freedom: Shota Aizawa (Eraser Head) expels students he judges hopeless and expelled his entire class last year. All Might is a famous hero but a beginner teacher; he reads from prepared notes and sometimes arrives late because he stopped incidents on the way. Many General Studies students resent the Hero Course, and some, Hitoshi Shinso among them, plan to use the Sports Festival to transfer in. Students know the grades and the rules; teachers also know the lockdown alarms and the Barrier's protocols; only Principal Nezu deals directly with the government and the Commission. Reporters often crowd the gate hoping to catch All Might, pestering anyone who comes or goes, and the faculty has little patience for them.

Hero Public Safety Commission.name: Hero Public Safety Commission
Hero Public Safety Commission.basicInfo: The government body that runs the hero system. It writes the rules for hero work, issues and revokes hero licenses, runs the Provisional Hero License Exam and coordinates heroes with the police. It also manages how the public sees heroes: it releases incident statistics, handles press relations and presents the twice-yearly Hero Billboard Chart JP, which ranks heroes by incidents resolved, public approval and social contribution. Its tower in central Tokyo is quiet, efficient and closed to visitors beyond the licensing counter. Heroes depend on it and rarely love it; to most citizens it is a seal on a license. The visible contradiction: a public-safety agency that worries about approval ratings as much as about safety.
Hero Public Safety Commission.hiddenInfo: Behind the counters, the Commission's first concern is public confidence in heroes, not any single case. Senior officials quietly settle hero property-damage claims, keep embarrassing incident reports out of the news and lean on heroes whose conduct hurts the system's image. Clerks and exam proctors believe in the rules they enforce and see little of this; the President and her senior staff decide what stays buried. Pressure is building: the Hero Killer, Stain, has murdered and crippled pro heroes in several cities, and every new attack dents public trust. The Commission shares its Hero Killer files with the police, and its exam office designs the Provisional Hero License Exam anew every year.

Japanese Police.name: Japanese Police
Japanese Police.basicInfo: The prefectural police forces under the National Police Agency: patrol officers, detectives, traffic and riot units, custody officers and prisoner transport. They investigate crimes, secure scenes, take statements and make arrests, but officers do not use their Quirks as weapons, so they rely on licensed heroes to stop villains in a fight. A typical incident ends with a hero restraining someone and an officer snapping on the handcuffs. Detective Naomasa Tsukauchi is a familiar face around Musutafu. Most people trust the police and barely notice them. The visible contradiction: officers hold the legal power to arrest, question and detain, yet heroes get the headlines, the rankings and the credit.
Japanese Police.hiddenInfo: Many officers resent the hero system's weight: budgets and attention follow heroes, arrests are reported as hero victories, and some heroes treat officers as a cleanup crew. Patrol officers know their streets; detectives work cases across prefectures and share files only with agencies they trust; senior officials at the National Police Agency coordinate policy with the Commission and know how much hero damage never reaches a courtroom. Detective Tsukauchi's Quirk tells him when a person is lying, which makes his interviews hard to fool. At the start of the year detectives in several prefectures are tracking the Hero Killer, Stain, along with a rise in seizures of Trigger, a street drug that boosts Quirks and wrecks judgment, in Kansai and around Tokyo.

League of Villains.name: League of Villains
League of Villains.basicInfo: A villain group so new and small that almost no one has heard of it. Its leader, Tomura Shigaraki, is a gaunt, restless young man who wears severed hands on his face and body, scratches his neck when frustrated and talks about villainy in video-game terms. Kurogiri, a polite man of dark mist whose Quirk opens warp gates, manages him, tends their hideout bar and moves people in and out. The rest are hired thugs found through brokers, and the man Shigaraki calls Sensei backs them all. Their aim is to kill All Might and bring down the hero society he holds up. The few brokers who deal with them see a strange client with money and big talk. The visible contradiction: a League with two real members at the start of the year, led by a man who has never led anyone.
League of Villains.hiddenInfo: The League is the project of the man Shigaraki calls Sensei, who speaks to them only as a voice through a screen in the bar. Kurogiri takes his orders from Sensei and keeps Tomura Shigaraki fed, focused and alive; Tomura follows his moods and thinks in levels, cheats and bosses. His touch with all five fingers turns anything to crumbling dust, people included. The hired thugs know only that the pay is good and the target is big; none of them has met Sensei, and few have seen the bar. The League buys muscle through brokers when it needs numbers, and Sensei has promised Tomura the weapon for killing All Might: hulking, silent creatures called Nomu, built to take All Might's blows. Tomura is impatient to use them.

Shie Hassaikai.name: Shie Hassaikai
Shie Hassaikai.basicInfo: One of the last yakuza houses in Japan, based in an old walled compound on the southeastern edge of Osaka. When heroes rose, they and the police broke the old crime families; the survivors were labeled designated villain groups and watched, and the Hassaikai has lasted by keeping its head down. Its old boss lies in a coma, and the house is run in his name by his young second, Kai Chisaki, called Overhaul: a cold, meticulous man in a beaked plague-doctor mask who cannot stand being touched and calls Quirks a sickness. His enforcers, the Eight Bullets, answer to him alone. Outsiders see a fading relic of the old underworld. The visible contradiction: everything is done in the boss's name, and the boss cannot speak.
Shie Hassaikai.hiddenInfo: Chisaki speaks of restoring the yakuza's standing for the boss's sake, but the boss fell into his coma soon after arguing with Chisaki over the house's direction, and the few who wonder how know better than to ask. His Quirk, also called Overhaul, takes apart and rebuilds whatever he touches, people included; he uses it to heal his loyalists and to kill. The rank and file still follow the old code and wait for the boss to wake; the Eight Bullets are sworn to Chisaki himself and carry out whatever he orders; his closest aide, Hari Kurono (Chronostasis), knows the most. Right now the house sells Trigger, a Quirk-boosting drug, through dealers and brokers across Kansai, and Chisaki is spending the profits on new muscle and on quiet approaches to other underworld groups.

Meta Liberation Army.name: Meta Liberation Army
Meta Liberation Army.basicInfo: A militant movement from the early years of the Quirk era. Led by a man called Destro, it demanded the right to use Quirks freely, calling every restriction an attack on a person's own body, and fought the government until it was crushed. Destro died in prison and the army was disbanded; today it shows up in documentaries and textbooks as a warning about Quirk extremism. Destro's writings still circulate among Quirk-rights activists and the curious. Officially it has had no members, no attacks and no leadership for decades, and most people file it under history. The visible contradiction: its central claim, that people should be free to use the power they were born with, still gets a sympathetic hearing on talk shows and online forums.
Meta Liberation Army.hiddenInfo: The army never ended; it went into business. Destro's son, Rikiya Yotsubashi, president of the support-equipment maker Detnerat, leads it as Re-Destro. It has more than a hundred thousand members across Japan, many placed in business, politics, the media and the support industry, and in Deika City nearly every resident belongs and drills for the day of liberation. Its four lieutenants are Geten, an ice user and true believer; Trumpet, a politician whose voice stirs crowds; Skeptic, an IT executive who runs its information network; and Curious, a journalist. Ordinary members know their local cell and the cause; the lieutenants know the membership; only Re-Destro decides when to act. Right now it is waiting: recruiting through Detnerat, meeting at a family villa on Gunga Mountain and watching the hero system for weakness.

Wild Wild Pussycats.name: Wild Wild Pussycats
Wild Wild Pussycats.basicInfo: A team of four pro heroes specializing in mountain rescue: Mandalay, whose Quirk lets her speak into many people's minds at once; Pixie-Bob, who shapes earth into moving beasts; Ragdoll, who can locate up to a hundred people and read their condition; and Tiger, a hard-hitting martial artist who can bend his body freely. They wear matching cat-themed costumes, strike a team pose whenever they introduce themselves and have worked together for well over a decade. Their lodge sits on their own land, a huge stretch of the Japanese Alps northwest of Musutafu, which U.A. uses for summer training camps. Outsiders see a cheerful, slightly old-fashioned idol team. The visible contradiction: behind the cat ears and the pose, most of their work is grim searches for people lost in the mountains.
Wild Wild Pussycats.hiddenInfo: Mountain rescue pays far less than city hero work and gets little airtime, so the U.A. camps and the team's public appearances keep its name alive. Mandalay looks after Kota Izumi, a small boy whose parents, the pro hero pair Water Hose, were killed in the line of duty two years ago by a villain who, as of the start of the year, has never been caught. Kota hates heroes, Quirks and anyone who admires them, and he disappears into the hills for hours; the team lets him, within limits. Ragdoll's Search is rare enough that disaster teams call on her. The four share everything at the lodge, but Mandalay makes the calls in the field. Right now Pixie-Bob is rebuilding the forest training course after the spring thaw, and the team is checking which slopes and trails are safe for summer.

Endeavor Hero Agency.name: Endeavor Hero Agency
Endeavor Hero Agency.basicInfo: The agency of Endeavor (Enji Todoroki), the Number Two hero at the start of the year, run from a tower in central Tokyo. Endeavor holds the record for the most incidents resolved in Japan's history, and the agency is built for volume: dozens of sidekicks on rotating shifts, an operations floor that tracks incidents across the city in real time, and a training gym where everyone is expected to keep pace. Sidekicks such as Burnin, Kido and Onima work in his shadow and know that his standards do not bend. The public respects his results and does not much like him: he ignores fans, refuses interviews he considers pointless and treats second place as an insult. The visible contradiction: the country's most effective hero is also one of its least loved.
Endeavor Hero Agency.hiddenInfo: Everything in the agency serves one goal: surpassing All Might. Endeavor never has, and he treats every chart at Number Two as a personal failure. His youngest son, Shoto Todoroki, began at U.A. Academy this April; Endeavor calls him his masterpiece, the one who will surpass All Might, while Shoto refuses to use his father's fire in a fight and barely speaks to him. Sidekicks see the drive and the temper; senior staff handle property-damage complaints and reporters asking about the family; nobody at the agency mentions Endeavor's wife, Rei Todoroki, hospitalized for years. Endeavor pushes the agency to take more cases every year and follows Shoto's progress at U.A. closely, expecting him to outshine every classmate.

Shiketsu Academy.name: Shiketsu Academy
Shiketsu Academy.basicInfo: The great hero academy of western Japan and U.A.'s closest rival: people speak of U.A. in the east and Shiketsu in the west. It trains high-school graduates over three years and is nearly as hard to enter. Its students wear dark formal uniforms with peaked caps, keep strict manners in public and train in rescue, teamwork and public conduct as hard as in combat; Shiketsu teaches that a hero's image is part of the job. Its first-years include Inasa Yoarashi, a huge, loud young man with a powerful wind Quirk who turned down a place at U.A. Outsiders see polished, reliable future heroes. The visible contradiction: an academy built on composure and modesty puts real energy into proving it is better than U.A.
Shiketsu Academy.hiddenInfo: Shiketsu's polish has a cost. Students police one another's manners closely, Seiji Shishikura among the strictest, and anyone who embarrasses the academy in public faces discipline. The rivalry with U.A. is also about money and influence: both academies compete for the best applicants, government funding and the Commission's goodwill. Inasa Yoarashi topped U.A.'s recommendation exam, then refused the place after a cold brush-off from Shoto Todoroki, whose eyes reminded him of Endeavor, a hero he despises; he has not let it go. Ordinary students see the rivalry as pride; the faculty see it as funding. Its first-years train for the Provisional Hero License Exam from their first term, and the faculty expect every one of them to pass on the first attempt.

Villain Brokers.name: Villain Brokers
Villain Brokers.basicInfo: Not one organization but a trade: the middlemen of Japan's underworld. Brokers sell introductions between villains and clients, rent out safe rooms and hideouts, supply forged IDs, unregistered support gear and weapons, and find hired muscle for anyone who pays. They work by burner phone from bar back rooms and pawnshops in port and nightlife districts. The best known is Giran, a smooth, sharp-dressed broker who has outlasted most of his clients by never taking sides. The police know many brokers' names and can prove little. To the few outsiders aware of them, brokers are shady businessmen. The visible contradiction: brokers rarely commit a crime themselves, yet almost no villain operation happens without one.
Villain Brokers.hiddenInfo: Brokers live on trust and leverage. Each keeps track of who owes what to whom, and the unwritten rule is never to sell a client's location; in practice some trade small tips to detectives to stay out of jail, and everyone knows it. Street fixers know a few dozen faces; Giran knows nearly everyone worth knowing and keeps his records far from his office. The Shie Hassaikai moves Trigger through brokers in Kansai, which the old hands dislike because drugs draw heroes. A newer client pays well above the going rate for hired muscle and asks for no names, and brokers around Kamino and Yokohama take the money while asking each other who has that kind of cash.

Hawks Hero Agency.name: Hawks Hero Agency
Hawks Hero Agency.basicInfo: The agency of Hawks, the Number Three hero at the start of the year, based in Fukuoka. Hawks is the youngest hero ever to reach the top ten: a quick, easygoing man in his mid-twenties with large crimson wings whose feathers he can detach and steer one by one, fine enough to sense vibrations and strong enough to carry people. He is so fast that his own sidekicks often arrive only to file the paperwork. The agency is small and lean: a handful of sidekicks, a dispatch desk and a press office answering questions about cases he closed an hour ago. Fans love his relaxed manner and his line that he wants a world where heroes have free time. The visible contradiction: the hero who talks about slowing down is the fastest worker in the country.
Hawks Hero Agency.hiddenInfo: Hawks keeps the agency small so nothing slows him down. He is rarely in the office and patrols from the air across Fukuoka and northern Kyushu, so the sidekicks spend their days on reports, press calls, crowd control and reaching scenes he has already cleared. Senior sidekicks run the office and decide which calls reach him; newer ones mostly handle crowds. Some admire him; a few feel useless and have asked for transfers. Behind the easy grin he reads people quickly and gives little away. His feathers burn easily, so fire is the one thing he plans around. Right now Fukuoka's small-time villains are moving their business out of the city to stay clear of him, and the coastal towns around it are seeing more Quirk crime than their local agencies can handle.
